structure.text:
Jin Zheng<sup>+</sup>, Mingxue Tang<sup>+</sup>, and Yan-Yan Hu\*

Abstract: Polymer-ceramic composite electrolytes are emerging as a promising solution to deliver high ionic conductivity, optimal mechanical properties, and good safety for developing high-performance all-solid-state rechargeable batteries. Composite electrolytes have been prepared with cubic-phase Li<sub>7</sub>La<sub>3</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>12</sub> (LLZO) garnet and polyethylene oxide (PEO) and employed in symmetric lithium battery cells. By combining selective isotope labeling and high-resolution solid-state Li NMR, we are able to track Li ion pathways within LLZO-PEO composite electrolytes by monitoring the replacement of <sup>7</sup>Li in the composite electrolyte by <sup>6</sup>Li from the <sup>6</sup>Li metal electrodes during battery cycling. We have provided the first experimental evidence to show that Li ions favor the pathway through the LLZO ceramic phase instead of the PEO-LLZO interface or PEO. This approach can be widely applied to study ion pathways in ionic conductors and to provide useful insights for developing composite materials for energy storage and harvesting.

Rechargeable lithium ion batteries (LIBs) are one of the leading technologies for energy storage.<sup>[1,2]</sup> Developing suitable electrolytes for high-voltage, high-energy-density, and safe LIBs is important yet challenging. [3,4] Electrolytes commonly employed in LIBs are dissolved in organic solvents, which are flammable and often decompose at high voltages. In addition, Li dendrite growth across liquid-based electrolytes causes safety issues and limits the utilization of Li metal as anodes.<sup>[5-7]</sup> To overcome these challenges, nonflammable solid-state electrolytes are suitable alternatives to organic-solvent-based electrolytes.[8-14] Inorganic ceramics and organic polymers are two general classes of materials used as solid electrolytes for LIBs. Among all inorganic ceramics, garnet-type electrolytes show very high ionic conductivity and chemical stability. For instance, cubicphase Li<sub>7</sub>La<sub>3</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>12</sub> (LLZO) exhibited an ionic conductivity of  $\sigma_{\text{bulk}} \approx 10^{-4} \, \text{S} \, \text{cm}$  at room temperature with superior stability[15] and a wide electrochemical voltage window.[16-18] However, ceramic materials are often too rigid and brittle, and show poor contact with electrodes. [19,20] Flexible polymer electrolytes exhibit more suitable mechanical properties than ceramics, but show low ionic conductivity at room temperature and poor stability at high temperatures. [21,22] Polyethylene oxide (PEO)-based materials are widely considered as promising candidates for LIBs because of their compatibility with lithium salts and low cost. [23,24] The combination of ceramics and polymers offers a new path to create better electrolytes with both high ionic conductivity and good mechanical properties.

Ionic conductivity of composite electrolytes is critical to their applications in all-solid-state rechargeable batteries. The ratio and integration of polymer and ceramics in composite electrolytes strongly affect their properties and performance. Significant improvement in the ionic conductivity of polymer electrolytes was obtained with the addition of ceramic particles.<sup>[25-27]</sup> It was suggested that an amorphous polymer shell formed around filler particles accounts for the increase in ionic conductivity.<sup>[9,28-30]</sup> Finite element simulations also revealed<sup>[28-30]</sup> that ion conduction within composite electrolytes mainly occurs at the ceramic–polymer interface. However, other hypotheses suggested that Li ions diffuse through the ceramic particles.<sup>[20,31]</sup> Experimental evidence is needed to resolve the debate surrounding Li ion pathways in composite materials.

As a very light element, Li is difficult to characterize with electron- or X-ray-based techniques. The polymer-ceramic composite electrolyte adds another layer of complexity for tracking Li ion diffusion. Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) has proven to be a powerful tool to study local structural environments and dynamics of Li ions.[32-38] To this end, we first apply high-resolution solid-state Li NMR to determine the local structural environments of Li ions in the PEO polymer, the LLZO ceramic phase, and at the LLZO-PEO interface. Both <sup>7</sup>Li and <sup>6</sup>Li are NMR active isotopes, which allow a unique way for probing Li ion transport pathways within composite electrolytes using isotope exchange. To determine possible lithium ion pathways, a symmetric battery made with 6Li-labeled lithium foils sandwiching a LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite electrolyte film was electrochemically cycled. In this symmetric battery, <sup>6</sup>Li ions were stripped from one <sup>6</sup>Li electrode into the electrolyte by electric potential, and then diffused through the electrolyte to deposit onto the other <sup>6</sup>Li electrode. Meanwhile, <sup>6</sup>Li ions partially replace <sup>7</sup>Li ions inside the electrolyte every time they move through the electrolyte, leaving a trail for the Li ion pathway. By comparing <sup>6</sup>Li and <sup>7</sup>Li NMR of pristine and cycled composite electrolytes, we are able to reveal Li ion pathways within the composite electrolyte.

The procedure for making the composite electrolyte is depicted in Figure 1. Symmetric lithium batteries were assembled with as-prepared composite electrolytes and <sup>6</sup>Li metal foils.

In the illustration, the blue area represents the PEO polymer matrix, red filled circles are LLZO particles, and the white regions represent the interface between PEO and LLZO.

NMR is sensitive to local structural environments and therefore can be used to distinguish Li ions in the polymer phase, the ceramic phase, and at the polymer-ceramic interface within composite electrolytes. For this purpose, <sup>6</sup>Li NMR is preferred for its much higher resolution compared to <sup>7</sup>Li NMR because strong <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interactions significantly broaden <sup>7</sup>Li resonances and result in overlapped peaks in <sup>7</sup>Li NMR. <sup>7</sup>Li NMR was employed for spin exchange experiments, which take advantage of strong <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interactions.

Possible Li local environments within the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite electrolyte are depicted in Figure 2a. High-resolution <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra of LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composites are shown in Figure 2b-d. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra of pure LLZO and LiClO<sub>4</sub> in PEO polymer (Figure 2b) were used as references. A single  $^6$ Li resonance at -0.2 ppm was observed for LiClO<sub>4</sub> within the PEO polymer matrix and at 2 ppm for Li in pure cubic-LLZO (Figure 2b, bottom). In the <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite, in addition to the -0.2 ppm and 2.0 ppm peaks, a third component at around 1.4 ppm (shown as a broad shoulder of the LLZO peak) was assigned to Li at the PEO and LLZO interface. In general, a longer CP contact time allows for greater polarization transfer from <sup>1</sup>H to <sup>6</sup>Li. The CP process is driven by dipolar coupling interactions between <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>6</sup>Li spins, which strongly depend on the <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li distance. Therefore, the LiClO<sub>4</sub> (in PEO) signal is preferentially enhanced (19.5 mol %) due to a shorter average LiClO<sub>4</sub>-PEO distance, Li in LLZO is underrepresented due to a longer <sup>1</sup>H PEO-LLZO distance, and the interfacial <sup>7</sup>Li stays more or less the same (19.1 mol%) in the <sup>6</sup>Li CP spectrum (Figure 2d). This confirmed the assignment of interfacial Li in the <sup>6</sup>Li spectra of LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composites.

The intensity increase of the LiClO<sub>4</sub> resonance (in the PEO phase), LLZO, and interfacial Li as a function of contact time was plotted individually and shown in Figure 3b. In principle, the LiClO<sup>4</sup> signal should reach the maximum first due to the shortest distance to <sup>1</sup>H within PEO. However, the result shows a relatively slow buildup for the LiClO<sup>4</sup> component (Figure 3 b), likely owing to the fast tumbling motion of small Li ions in LiClO<sup>4</sup> which weakens the <sup>1</sup>H@<sup>6</sup>Li dipolar coupling and makes the CP process less efficient. <sup>1</sup>H@<sup>6</sup>Li CP NMR on cycled LLZO-PEO electrolytes (Figures S1 and S2) also confirmed the assignment of interfacial Li resonances.

The relative spatial disposition of different Li components can also be probed with <sup>7</sup>Li 2D exchange spectroscopy (EXSY).[39] A cross peak in a 2D EXSY spectrum at frequency coordinates (dA, dB) indicates in general that the spin resonating at dA is interacting with, and thus spatially close to, the spin resonating at dB. Figure 4 a shows an example of <sup>7</sup>Li 2D-EXSY spectra for pristine LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composites. In the contour plot (Figure 4 a), the two circle regions located on the diagonal are peaks from LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> inside PEO, respectively. The region between LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> peaks on the diagonal in the 2D EXSY spectrum is from interfacial Li. In 2D EXSY experiments, a mixing time period is set to allow spin interactions among LLZO, LiClO<sup>4</sup> , and interfacial Li. Longer mixing times often permit spin interactions over a larger spatial range. If spin interactions occur, off-diagonal peaks (also known as cross peaks) will show in the 2D EXSY spectra that connect the two interactive components. To more clearly observe the spin exchange process, 1D cross sections were taken at the chemical shift of LiClO<sup>4</sup> from the 2D EXSY spectra (as indicated by the horizontal dashed line) with mixing times of 0.0001, 0.05, 0.4, and 1.0 s. These 1D cross-section spectra (in Figure 4 b) reveal all of the other components that interact with LiClO<sup>4</sup> due to spatial vicinity. At a very short mixing time of 0.1 ms, only the LiClO<sup>4</sup> peak was observed (blue). Upon gradual increase of the mixing time up to 1.0 s, the <sup>6</sup>Li peak at 1.4 ppm from the interfacial Li grew stronger, suggesting spin exchange between LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO and interfacial Li. No spin exchange between LiClO<sup>4</sup> and LLZO was observed owing to their relatively large distance apart. In summary, the 2D <sup>7</sup>Li EXSY experiments of LLZO-PEO composites confirm the <sup>6</sup>Li resonance assignment of interfacial Li at 1.4 ppm.

So far, a clear assignment of Li in the PEO phase, Li in LLZO, and interfacial Li has been made and confirmed. The interfacial Li resonance is significantly broader than LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO, indicating a larger degree of structural disorder at the interface. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR chemical shift of interfacial Li (1.4 ppm) is very close to that of Li from LLZO (2.0 ppm), which suggests that interfacial Li is from the LLZO surface and is heavily affected by PEO matrix.

To probe Li<sup>+</sup> ion pathways within the LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolyte during battery cycling, a symmetric battery was assembled with LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) electrolyte and <sup>6</sup>Li metal electrodes (Figure 5 a). The symmetric cell was cycled using a constant current density of 61 mA cm@<sup>2</sup> and a slightly biased potential that changed sign every 5 min. Upon battery cycling, <sup>6</sup>Li ions move from one electrode, across the composite electrolyte, to the other electrode. On their way, <sup>6</sup>Li ions replace <sup>7</sup>Li ions in the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) composite electrolyte, leaving a trail of the diffusion pathway. By comparing the <sup>6</sup>Li spectra of the composite electrolyte before and after electrochemical cycling, an increase in the <sup>6</sup>Li peak intensity can be observed for those Li local environments where <sup>6</sup>Li ions pass. As shown in Figure 5 c, the <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the cycled composite electrolyte showed significantly increased intensity for the LLZO peak, and only a slight increase for the interfacial Li and LiClO<sup>4</sup> resonances compared with that of the pristine LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite. This indicates that a large amount of <sup>6</sup>Li replaced <sup>7</sup>Li within LLZO. The replacement could be further quantified based on spectral simulation (Figure 5 d). The peak intensity of LLZO increased by 39%, only a 6% increment was found for interfacial Li, and there was very little or no increase for LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO. Complementary <sup>7</sup>Li spectra of pristine and cycled LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolytes show decreased intensity of <sup>7</sup>Li LLZO resonance, confirming the replacement of <sup>7</sup>Li by passing <sup>6</sup>Li ions in the LLZO phase (Figure S3). Additionally, a <sup>7</sup>Li foil/composite electrolyte/<sup>7</sup>Li foil symmetric battery was assembled and cycled under the same condition as for the <sup>6</sup>Li symmetric cell. A slightly increased <sup>7</sup>Li signal was only observed for the LLZO peak after cycling (Figure S3); this is

The results obtained from the <sup>7</sup>Li symmetric cell further confirmed that Li ions diffuse through LLZO particles, consistent with the investigation using the <sup>6</sup>Li symmetric cell. Possible Li ion pathways are indicated in Figure 5 a. In summary, the 6,7Li NMR results show that Li ions prefer to go through LLZO particles and minimize the fraction of polymer phase or interface on their pathway when possible. LLZO accounts for about 20 vol% in the composite electrolytes; in order to allow Li ion transport to largely occur in the LLZO phase, LLZO particles need to form a percolation network.

In conclusion, various Li local structural environments within LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) composite electrolytes have been resolved by 1D high-resolution <sup>6</sup>Li NMR. <sup>6</sup>Li CP and <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY NMR confirmed the assignment of NMR resonance for interfacial Li. The replacement of <sup>7</sup>Li by <sup>6</sup>Li ions in the LLZO ceramic phase of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolyte, when used in a symmetric ( <sup>6</sup>Li electrode/composite electrolyte/<sup>6</sup>Li electrode) battery cell, indicates that Li ions prefer to maximize the fraction of the LLZO ceramic phase and minimize that of the interface or the PEO polymer phase on their diffusion pathway. We have succeeded in employing Li NMR to probe Li ion diffusion pathway within LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolytes employed in all-solid-state batteries. Our study provides the first experimental evidence to show that Li ions mainly pass through LLZO ceramic particles, not the interface or the PEO polymer phase. The method used here, that is, using NMR active isotopes of the same element to track ion diffusion pathway, can be widely applied in materials and chemistry research.

nodes.title: Introduction and Background on Solid-State Electrolytes
nodes.text: Rechargeable lithium ion batteries (LIBs) are one of the leading technologies for energy storage.<sup>[1,2]</sup> Developing suitable electrolytes for high-voltage, high-energy-density, and safe LIBs is important yet challenging. [3,4] Electrolytes commonly employed in LIBs are dissolved in organic solvents, which are flammable and often decompose at high voltages. In addition, Li dendrite growth across liquid-based electrolytes causes safety issues and limits the utilization of Li metal as anodes.<sup>[5-7]</sup> To overcome these challenges, nonflammable solid-state electrolytes are suitable alternatives to organic-solvent-based electrolytes.[8-14] Inorganic ceramics and organic polymers are two general classes of materials used as solid electrolytes for LIBs. Among all inorganic ceramics, garnet-type electrolytes show very high ionic conductivity and chemical stability. For instance, cubicphase Li<sub>7</sub>La<sub>3</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>12</sub> (LLZO) exhibited an ionic conductivity of  $\sigma_{\text{bulk}} \approx 10^{-4} \, \text{S} \, \text{cm}$  at room temperature with superior stability[15] and a wide electrochemical voltage window.[16-18] However, ceramic materials are often too rigid and brittle, and show poor contact with electrodes. [19,20] Flexible polymer electrolytes exhibit more suitable mechanical properties than ceramics, but show low ionic conductivity at room temperature and poor stability at high temperatures. [21,22] Polyethylene oxide (PEO)-based materials are widely considered as promising candidates for LIBs because of their compatibility with lithium salts and low cost. [23,24] The combination of ceramics and polymers offers a new path to create better electrolytes with both high ionic conductivity and good mechanical properties. Ionic conductivity of composite electrolytes is critical to their applications in all-solid-state rechargeable batteries. The ratio and integration of polymer and ceramics in composite electrolytes strongly affect their properties and performance. Significant improvement in the ionic conductivity of polymer electrolytes was obtained with the addition of ceramic particles.<sup>[25-27]</sup> It was suggested that an amorphous polymer shell formed around filler particles accounts for the increase in ionic conductivity.<sup>[9,28-30]</sup> Finite element simulations also revealed<sup>[28-30]</sup> that ion conduction within composite electrolytes mainly occurs at the ceramic–polymer interface. However, other hypotheses suggested that Li ions diffuse through the ceramic particles.<sup>[20,31]</sup> Experimental evidence is needed to resolve the debate surrounding Li ion pathways in composite materials.

nodes.title: General Methodology for Ion Pathway Tracking
nodes.text: As a very light element, Li is difficult to characterize with electron- or X-ray-based techniques. The polymer-ceramic composite electrolyte adds another layer of complexity for tracking Li ion diffusion. Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) has proven to be a powerful tool to study local structural environments and dynamics of Li ions.[32-38] To this end, we first apply high-resolution solid-state Li NMR to determine the local structural environments of Li ions in the PEO polymer, the LLZO ceramic phase, and at the LLZO-PEO interface. Both <sup>7</sup>Li and <sup>6</sup>Li are NMR active isotopes, which allow a unique way for probing Li ion transport pathways within composite electrolytes using isotope exchange. To determine possible lithium ion pathways, a symmetric battery made with 6Li-labeled lithium foils sandwiching a LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite electrolyte film was electrochemically cycled. In this symmetric battery, <sup>6</sup>Li ions were stripped from one <sup>6</sup>Li electrode into the electrolyte by electric potential, and then diffused through the electrolyte to deposit onto the other <sup>6</sup>Li electrode. Meanwhile, <sup>6</sup>Li ions partially replace <sup>7</sup>Li ions inside the electrolyte every time they move through the electrolyte, leaving a trail for the Li ion pathway. By comparing <sup>6</sup>Li and <sup>7</sup>Li NMR of pristine and cycled composite electrolytes, we are able to reveal Li ion pathways within the composite electrolyte.

nodes.title: NMR Characterization, Peak Assignments, and CP-NMR Confirmation
nodes.text:
NMR is sensitive to local structural environments and therefore can be used to distinguish Li ions in the polymer phase, the ceramic phase, and at the polymer-ceramic interface within composite electrolytes. For this purpose, <sup>6</sup>Li NMR is preferred for its much higher resolution compared to <sup>7</sup>Li NMR because strong <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interactions significantly broaden <sup>7</sup>Li resonances and result in overlapped peaks in <sup>7</sup>Li NMR. <sup>7</sup>Li NMR was employed for spin exchange experiments, which take advantage of strong <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interactions. Possible Li local environments within the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite electrolyte are depicted in Figure 2a. High-resolution <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra of LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composites are shown in Figure 2b-d. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra of pure LLZO and LiClO<sub>4</sub> in PEO polymer (Figure 2b) were used as references. A single  $^6$ Li resonance at -0.2 ppm was observed for LiClO<sub>4</sub> within the PEO polymer matrix and at 2 ppm for Li in pure cubic-LLZO (Figure 2b, bottom). In the <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sub>4</sub>) composite, in addition to the -0.2 ppm and 2.0 ppm peaks, a third component at around 1.4 ppm (shown as a broad shoulder of the LLZO peak) was assigned to Li at the PEO and LLZO interface. In principle, the LiClO<sup>4</sup> signal should reach the maximum first due to the shortest distance to <sup>1</sup>H within PEO. However, the result shows a relatively slow buildup for the LiClO<sup>4</sup> component (Figure 3 b), likely owing to the fast tumbling motion of small Li ions in LiClO<sup>4</sup> which weakens the <sup>1</sup>H@<sup>6</sup>Li dipolar coupling and makes the CP process less efficient. <sup>1</sup>H@<sup>6</sup>Li CP NMR on cycled LLZO-PEO electrolytes (Figures S1 and S2) also confirmed the assignment of interfacial Li resonances. The relative spatial disposition of different Li components can also be probed with <sup>7</sup>Li 2D exchange spectroscopy (EXSY).[39] A cross peak in a 2D EXSY spectrum at frequency coordinates (dA, dB) indicates in general that the spin resonating at dA is interacting with, and thus spatially close to, the spin resonating at dB. Figure 4 a shows an example of <sup>7</sup>Li 2D-EXSY spectra for pristine LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composites. In the contour plot (Figure 4 a), the two circle regions located on the diagonal are peaks from LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> inside PEO, respectively. The region between LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> peaks on the diagonal in the 2D EXSY spectrum is from interfacial Li. In 2D EXSY experiments, a mixing time period is set to allow spin interactions among LLZO, LiClO<sup>4</sup> , and interfacial Li. Longer mixing times often permit spin interactions over a larger spatial range. If spin interactions occur, off-diagonal peaks (also known as cross peaks) will show in the 2D EXSY spectra that connect the two interactive components. To more clearly observe the spin exchange process, 1D cross sections were taken at the chemical shift of LiClO<sup>4</sup> from the 2D EXSY spectra (as indicated by the horizontal dashed line) with mixing times of 0.0001, 0.05, 0.4, and 1.0 s. These 1D cross-section spectra (in Figure 4 b) reveal all of the other components that interact with LiClO<sup>4</sup> due to spatial vicinity. At a very short mixing time of 0.1 ms, only the LiClO<sup>4</sup> peak was observed (blue). Upon gradual increase of the mixing time up to 1.0 s, the <sup>6</sup>Li peak at 1.4 ppm from the interfacial Li grew stronger, suggesting spin exchange between LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO and interfacial Li. No spin exchange between LiClO<sup>4</sup> and LLZO was observed owing to their relatively large distance apart. In summary, the 2D <sup>7</sup>Li EXSY experiments of LLZO-PEO composites confirm the <sup>6</sup>Li resonance assignment of interfacial Li at 1.4 ppm. So far, a clear assignment of Li in the PEO phase, Li in LLZO, and interfacial Li has been made and confirmed. The interfacial Li resonance is significantly broader than LLZO and LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO, indicating a larger degree of structural disorder at the interface. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR chemical shift of interfacial Li (1.4 ppm) is very close to that of Li from LLZO (2.0 ppm), which suggests that interfacial Li is from the LLZO surface and is heavily affected by PEO matrix.

nodes.title: Experimental Tracking of Li Ion Diffusion Pathways and Quantitative Results
nodes.text: To probe Li<sup>+</sup> ion pathways within the LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolyte during battery cycling, a symmetric battery was assembled with LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) electrolyte and <sup>6</sup>Li metal electrodes (Figure 5 a). The symmetric cell was cycled using a constant current density of 61 mA cm@<sup>2</sup> and a slightly biased potential that changed sign every 5 min. Upon battery cycling, <sup>6</sup>Li ions move from one electrode, across the composite electrolyte, to the other electrode. On their way, <sup>6</sup>Li ions replace <sup>7</sup>Li ions in the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) composite electrolyte, leaving a trail of the diffusion pathway. By comparing the <sup>6</sup>Li spectra of the composite electrolyte before and after electrochemical cycling, an increase in the <sup>6</sup>Li peak intensity can be observed for those Li local environments where <sup>6</sup>Li ions pass. As shown in Figure 5 c, the <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the cycled composite electrolyte showed significantly increased intensity for the LLZO peak, and only a slight increase for the interfacial Li and LiClO<sup>4</sup> resonances compared with that of the pristine LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite. This indicates that a large amount of <sup>6</sup>Li replaced <sup>7</sup>Li within LLZO. The replacement could be further quantified based on spectral simulation (Figure 5 d). The peak intensity of LLZO increased by 39%, only a 6% increment was found for interfacial Li, and there was very little or no increase for LiClO<sup>4</sup> in PEO. Complementary <sup>7</sup>Li spectra of pristine and cycled LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolytes show decreased intensity of <sup>7</sup>Li LLZO resonance, confirming the replacement of <sup>7</sup>Li by passing <sup>6</sup>Li ions in the LLZO phase (Figure S3). Additionally, a <sup>7</sup>Li foil/composite electrolyte/<sup>7</sup>Li foil symmetric battery was assembled and cycled under the same condition as for the <sup>6</sup>Li symmetric cell. A slightly increased <sup>7</sup>Li signal was only observed for the LLZO peak after cycling (Figure S3); this is __IMG_06d11aa2__ __IMG_58d8b365__ __IMG_96403e19__ Figure 5. a) Illustration of the symmetric <sup>6</sup> Li foil/composite electrolyte/ 6 Li foil battery and possible Li<sup>+</sup> transport pathways within the composite electrolyte upon cycling the symmetric battery. b) Electrochemical profile of the symmetric lithium battery cycled with a constant current that changes signs every 300 s. c) Comparison of the <sup>6</sup> Li NMR spectra of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) composite electrolytes before (pristine) and after (cycled) cycling. d) Quantitative analysis of <sup>6</sup> Li amount in LiClO<sup>4</sup> , interface, and LLZO of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) before and after cycling. because <sup>7</sup>Li ions replace <sup>6</sup>Li (7.6 atom% natural abundance) on their way through the electrolyte. The results obtained from the <sup>7</sup>Li symmetric cell further confirmed that Li ions diffuse through LLZO particles, consistent with the investigation using the <sup>6</sup>Li symmetric cell. Possible Li ion pathways are indicated in Figure 5 a. In summary, the 6,7Li NMR results show that Li ions prefer to go through LLZO particles and minimize the fraction of polymer phase or interface on their pathway when possible. LLZO accounts for about 20 vol% in the composite electrolytes; in order to allow Li ion transport to largely occur in the LLZO phase, LLZO particles need to form a percolation network.

nodes.title: Conclusion and Broader Implications
nodes.text: In conclusion, various Li local structural environments within LLZO-PEO (LiClO<sup>4</sup> ) composite electrolytes have been resolved by 1D high-resolution <sup>6</sup>Li NMR. <sup>6</sup>Li CP and <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY NMR confirmed the assignment of NMR resonance for interfacial Li. The replacement of <sup>7</sup>Li by <sup>6</sup>Li ions in the LLZO ceramic phase of the LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolyte, when used in a symmetric ( <sup>6</sup>Li electrode/composite electrolyte/<sup>6</sup>Li electrode) battery cell, indicates that Li ions prefer to maximize the fraction of the LLZO ceramic phase and minimize that of the interface or the PEO polymer phase on their diffusion pathway. We have succeeded in employing Li NMR to probe Li ion diffusion pathway within LLZO-PEO (LiClO4) composite electrolytes employed in all-solid-state batteries. Our study provides the first experimental evidence to show that Li ions mainly pass through LLZO ceramic particles, not the interface or the PEO polymer phase. The method used here, that is, using NMR active isotopes of the same element to track ion diffusion pathway, can be widely applied in materials and chemistry research.

structure.title: Experimental Section
structure.text:
Cubic LLZO (Li7La3Zr2O12) garnet was synthesized with solid-state reactions using 19.8 wt% LiOH (Sigma–Aldrich, + 98%; pre-dried at 2008C for 6 h; 52.5 wt% La2O<sup>3</sup> (Sigma–Aldrich, + 99.9%; pre-dried at 9008C for 12 h), 26.5 wt% ZrO<sup>2</sup> (Sigma–Aldrich, + 99%), and 1.2 wt% Al2O<sup>3</sup> . The mixed powder was ball-milled for 0.5 h using a SPEX SamplePrep 8000M mixer/mill. The mixture was then calcined at 8008C for 12 h. After cooling down, the powder was reground and pressed into a pellet, which was sintered at 10008C for 36 h and crushed into powder again by ball–milling for 1 h.

The composite electrolyte was prepared with a solution-casting method. PEO (Sigma–Aldrich, MW= 400000) and LiClO<sup>4</sup> (Sigma– Aldrich, + 99.99%; vacuum dried at 1008C for 24 h) were dissolved in anhydrous acetonitrile by stirring at 808C for 12 h in an argon-filled glovebox. The [EO]/[Li] ratio was fixed at 18:1, and the amount of LLZO powder added was 50 wt%, corresponding to 20 vol%. The PEO/LiClO<sup>4</sup> /acetonitrile solution and LLZO powder were mixed by ball-milling for 1 h. The homogeneous slurry was cast on a flat Teflon plate using a doctor blade. The film was dried in vacuum at 508C for 12 h. The thickness of the composite electrolyte ranged from 30 mm to 50 mm.

The symmetric battery cell was assembled by pressing Li foils on both sides of the composite electrolyte film. Charge and discharge cycling of the symmetric cell was conducted at a constant current density of 61 mA cm @2 on a LANHE battery testing system.

Solid-state NMR spectra were acquired on a Bruker Avance III-500 at Larmor frequencies of 73.6 and 194.4 MHz for <sup>6</sup>Li and <sup>7</sup>Li, respectively. A 2.5 mm Bruker HXY probe was used and the samples were spun at 25 kHz for DP and 10 kHz for CP. The 6,7Li chemical shift was referenced to solid LiCl at 0 ppm.
